tips.title: Double it and add two
tips.body: The alkane formula is $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$: count the carbons, **double**, **add two**. Six carbons means fourteen hydrogens. It also tells you what is **not** an alkane: C₄H₈ is two hydrogens short.

tips.title: Two rise, one falls
tips.body: As molecules get **bigger**: boiling point **up**, viscosity **up**, flammability **down**. Only flammability falls. Petrol is small, runny and easy to light; heavy fuel oil is big, thick and hard to light.

tips.title: Balance carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
tips.body: Always in that order. Carbon fixes the CO₂, hydrogen fixes the H₂O, then count the oxygen atoms on the right and halve to get the O₂. If halving leaves a **half**, double every coefficient. Oxygen goes last because it appears in **both** products.

tips.title: Boiling separates molecules, not bonds
tips.body: When a hydrocarbon boils, the **forces between molecules** are overcome. The **covalent bonds inside** each molecule stay intact. An answer saying the bonds break loses the mark, however right the rest of it is.

why.matters:
Crude oil is a mixture of thousands of compounds and useless as it comes out of the ground. Everything that makes it valuable is **separation** — and the property that lets you separate it is the one that changes steadily with the size of the molecule.

That is why this topic pairs a homologous series with fractional distillation. Longer molecules mean stronger forces between them, which means a higher boiling point, which means they condense lower down the column. One trend, and an industry built on it.

examples.title: Everything at a petrol station came out of one column
examples.body:
The bottled gas, the petrol, the diesel and the tar on the forecourt itself are all the same crude oil, separated by **boiling point** in a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top.

Short molecules have weak forces between them, boil easily and rise to the cool top before condensing. Long ones barely evaporate at all and run out of the bottom as bitumen. Nothing is made here and nothing reacts — the fractions were all in the barrel to begin with.

visual.alt: A table of the fractions from crude oil in order of chain length: refinery gases with one to four carbons for bottled gas, petrol with five to ten for cars, kerosene for aircraft, diesel for lorries, and bitumen with over thirty-five carbons for road surfaces

examples.title: Why a camping stove takes propane in winter
examples.body:
Butane and propane are the same family one carbon apart, and a gas bottle only works if its contents will **boil** at the temperature outside.

Butane boils at about **-0.5 °C**, so on a frosty morning it stays liquid in the bottle and the stove will not light. Propane boils at **-42 °C** and is still a gas far below freezing. One extra carbon means stronger forces between the molecules, and forty degrees of boiling point — which is why winter bottles are propane.

props.title: One carbon more, forty degrees of boiling point

visual.alt: The structures of propane and butane side by side, three carbons against four, with their boiling points of minus forty-two and about zero degrees Celsius: one extra carbon is forty degrees of difference

examples.title: Why there is no more being made
examples.body:
Crude oil is **finite**, and the reason is in how it formed: an ancient biomass, mainly plankton, that settled into mud and was buried, then left under heat and pressure for millions of years.

Nothing about that is happening on a useful timescale. Plankton are still dying and still sinking, but the oil being burned this year took longer to make than our species has existed. *Finite* in this topic is not a figure of speech — it is a statement about a rate.

visual.alt: A flow chart of how crude oil formed: plankton in an ancient sea buried in mud, then heat and pressure over millions of years, leaving crude oil trapped in rock

steps.title: What crude oil is
steps.body:
**Crude oil** is a **finite resource found in rocks**. It formed from the remains of an **ancient biomass**, consisting **mainly of plankton**, that was **buried in mud**.

Learn that sentence: *finite*, *plankton*, *buried in mud*. Questions ask for it almost word for word, and "dead dinosaurs" earns nothing.

Crude oil is a **mixture of a very large number of compounds**. Most of them are **hydrocarbons**, which are molecules **made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only**.

That word *only* is doing real work. A molecule containing oxygen, nitrogen or chlorine is **not** a hydrocarbon, however much carbon and hydrogen it also contains.

Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to a family called the **alkanes**.

steps.title: The alkanes
steps.body:
The alkanes are a **homologous series**: a family of similar compounds that follow one general formula.

$$\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$$

So count the carbons, double it, add two, and that is the number of hydrogens. The first four are the only names you need.

- **methane**, CH₄
- **ethane**, C₂H₆
- **propane**, C₃H₈
- **butane**, C₄H₁₀

You are **not** expected to know the names of any other specific alkanes.

What you are expected to do is **recognise** an alkane from its formula. Check it against $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$: C₁₀H₂₂ has ten carbons and $2 \times 10 + 2 = 22$ hydrogens, so it is an alkane. C₃H₆ has three carbons but only six hydrogens, where the formula demands eight, so it is not.

visuals.alt: A table of the first four alkanes with the number of carbon atoms and the formula each one gives

steps.text: Count the carbons: $n = 5$
The general formula needs $2n + 2 = 2 \times 5 + 2 = 12$ hydrogens
The molecule has 12 hydrogens, which matches
So **yes**, it is an alkane
You are not expected to name it: only methane, ethane, propane and butane are required

check.solution: The general formula is $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$. For four carbons that needs $2 \times 4 + 2 = 10$ hydrogens, so **C₄H₁₀** is the alkane. The others all have too few.

steps.title: Fractional distillation
steps.body:
Crude oil is useless as it comes: a mixture of thousands of compounds. It is separated by **fractional distillation** into **fractions**, each containing molecules with a **similar number of carbon atoms**.

The explanation must be in terms of **evaporation and condensation**, and the marks go in this order:

1. The crude oil is **heated** until most of it **evaporates**.
2. The vapours pass into a **fractionating column**, which is **hot at the bottom and cooler at the top**.
3. As a vapour rises it **cools**. When it reaches a level where the temperature is **below its boiling point**, it **condenses** and is collected.
4. Molecules with **high boiling points** condense **low down**; those with **low boiling points** rise **higher** before condensing, and the smallest leave as gases at the top.

So the column sorts by boiling point, and boiling point depends on molecule size. That is the whole idea.

The fractions are then processed into **fuels** and into **feedstock** for the **petrochemical industry**.

steps.title: How properties change with size
steps.body:
Three properties change as hydrocarbon molecules get **larger**, and the specification limits you to exactly these three.

- **Boiling point: increases.** Larger molecules have stronger forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate them.
- **Viscosity: increases.** Viscosity means how thick and sticky a liquid is, so larger molecules flow less easily.
- **Flammability: decreases.** Larger molecules are harder to ignite.

Two of the three go up and one goes down, which is why this gets muddled. The one that goes **down** is **flammability**.

These properties decide what each fraction is used for. Petrol has small molecules, so it is volatile and easily ignited, which suits a car engine. Heavy fuel oil has large molecules, so it is thick and hard to ignite, which suits a ship's engine but would be useless in a car.

steps.title: Combustion equations
steps.body:
Burning a hydrocarbon **releases energy**. During combustion the **carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised**.

**Complete** combustion, meaning plenty of oxygen, produces **carbon dioxide and water**, and nothing else.

$$\text{hydrocarbon} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

Balancing one is mechanical if you do it in a fixed order: **carbon first, hydrogen second, oxygen last**. Oxygen goes last because it appears in both products, so its total is only known once the others are settled.

visuals.problem: Balance the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈

steps.text: **Carbon**: 3 on the left, so 3 CO₂ on the right
**Hydrogen**: 8 on the left, so 4 H₂O, since each has 2
**Oxygen on the right**: $3 \times 2 + 4 = 10$ atoms
So 5 O₂ on the left, because each molecule has 2 atoms
$$C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O$$

steps.title: Going deeper: why the trends exist, and why they matter
steps.body:
Most answers state the trends. A top answer explains them and then uses them.

**Why boiling point rises with size.** Boiling means separating molecules from one another, and that means overcoming the **forces between molecules**. A larger molecule has more contact with its neighbours, so those forces are **stronger** and more energy is needed to overcome them. Notice what is *not* being broken: the covalent bonds **inside** each molecule stay intact when a hydrocarbon boils. Saying "the bonds break" loses the mark.

**Why that drives everything else.** Fractional distillation sorts by **boiling point**, so it is really sorting by **molecule size**. That is why each fraction contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms, and why the fractions differ so much in how they behave.

**Why it decides the use.** A fuel for a car must vaporise and ignite readily, which means small molecules. A lubricant must be thick and stay put, which means large ones. The property comes from the size, and the use comes from the property.

**Why carbon can do this at all.** The specification makes the point directly: the vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds exists because carbon atoms can form **families of similar compounds**. Alkanes are one such family, and the general formula is what makes a family a family.

One caution worth carrying. "Finite" means crude oil is **being used far faster than it forms**, so supplies will run out. It does not mean none is forming at all.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Crude oil** is a **finite resource found in rocks**, formed from an **ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud**.
- It is a **mixture of a very large number of compounds**, most of them **hydrocarbons**: hydrogen and carbon **only**.
- Most are **alkanes**, general formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$.
- The four you must name: **methane** CH₄, **ethane** C₂H₆, **propane** C₃H₈, **butane** C₄H₁₀.
- **Fractional distillation** separates crude oil into **fractions** with a **similar number of carbon atoms**, by **evaporation and condensation**.
- The column is **hot at the bottom, cooler at the top**. High boiling points condense **low**, low boiling points rise **high**.
- Fuels from crude oil: **petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil, liquefied petroleum gases**.
- The **petrochemical industry** makes **solvents, lubricants, polymers, detergents**.
- As molecules get larger: **boiling point increases**, **viscosity increases**, **flammability decreases**.
- **Combustion releases energy**, and the **carbon and hydrogen are oxidised**.
- **Complete combustion** gives **carbon dioxide and water**. Balance carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen.
- Boiling overcomes the forces **between** molecules; the covalent bonds **inside** them are not broken.

questions.prompt: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions, and explain why the fraction collected near the bottom of the column is more viscous than the one collected near the top.
questions.solution: Crude oil is first heated so that most of it evaporates, and the vapour is passed into a fractionating column which is hot at the bottom and cooler towards the top. As a vapour rises it cools, and when it reaches a level where the temperature has fallen below its boiling point it condenses and is collected as a fraction. Molecules with high boiling points therefore condense low down in the column, while molecules with low boiling points travel much further up before they condense, and the smallest leave the top as gases. Because boiling point increases with the size of the molecule, this sorts the mixture by molecule size, and each fraction contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms. The fraction collected near the bottom is therefore made of the largest molecules. Viscosity also increases with molecule size, because larger molecules have stronger forces between them and cannot flow past one another easily, so the fraction from the bottom of the column is much more viscous than the one from the top.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The separation.** The crude oil is **heated** so most of it **evaporates**, and the vapour enters a **fractionating column** that is **hot at the bottom and cooler at the top**. As a vapour rises it **cools**, and where the temperature falls **below its boiling point** it **condenses** and is collected.

So vapours with **high boiling points condense low down**, while those with **low boiling points** rise much higher, and the smallest leave the top as gases. Since boiling point rises with molecule size, the column is really sorting by **size**, which is why each fraction contains molecules with a **similar number of carbon atoms**.

**Why the bottom fraction is more viscous.** It contains the **largest** molecules. Viscosity also **increases** with molecule size, because larger molecules have **stronger forces between them** and cannot slide past one another easily.

questions.prompt: Petrol is used in car engines and heavy fuel oil is used in large ships. Using the properties of hydrocarbons, explain why each fuel suits its use.
questions.solution: Petrol is a fraction containing relatively small hydrocarbon molecules. Small molecules have a low boiling point, so petrol vaporises easily inside the engine, which it must do in order to mix with air and burn. They also give a low viscosity, so the fuel flows readily through narrow pipes and injectors without needing to be heated first. Most importantly, small molecules are highly flammable, so the fuel and air mixture ignites reliably from a spark thousands of times a minute, which is exactly what a car engine requires. Heavy fuel oil is a fraction containing much larger molecules, so all three properties go the other way. It has a high boiling point and does not vaporise easily, it is very viscous and often has to be heated before it will even flow through the pipes, and it has low flammability so it is difficult to ignite. Those properties would make it useless in a car, but a large ship has slow running engines, room for heating equipment and a need for a cheap fuel, so the drawbacks can be managed and the low cost becomes the deciding advantage.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Petrol: small molecules.**

- **Low boiling point**, so it vaporises easily in the engine and can mix with air.
- **Low viscosity**, so it flows through narrow pipes and injectors.
- **High flammability**, so the mixture ignites reliably from a spark thousands of times a minute.

**Heavy fuel oil: large molecules**, so every property goes the other way.

- **High boiling point**: it does not vaporise easily.
- **Very viscous**: it often has to be **heated** before it will flow.
- **Low flammability**: it is hard to ignite.

**Why the match works.** Those properties would make heavy fuel oil useless in a car. A large ship has slow-running engines, room for heating equipment and a strong need for a **cheap** fuel, so the drawbacks can be managed and the low cost decides it.

examTechnique.body:
Use the definitions the specification uses. Crude oil is a **finite resource found in rocks**, from an **ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud**. A hydrocarbon contains **hydrogen and carbon only**.

To test whether a formula is an alkane, apply $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ rather than guessing from the name.

For fractional distillation, give the sequence: heat, **evaporate**, rise, cool, **condense** where the temperature is below the boiling point. Mentioning evaporation and condensation by name is what the mark scheme wants.

For the trends, name all three and remember that only flammability falls.

For a combustion equation, balance **carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen**. If the oxygen comes out as a half, double everything.

For a question about why a fuel suits a use, go size, then property, then use. Skipping the middle step loses marks even when the conclusion is right.
examinerErrors: Saying crude oil formed from dinosaurs rather than from plankton buried in mud.
Calling any carbon compound a hydrocarbon. It must be hydrogen and carbon only.
Saying flammability increases with molecule size. It decreases.
Explaining boiling by saying the covalent bonds break. The forces between molecules are overcome instead.
Balancing oxygen before hydrogen, so the equation has to be redone.
Describing fractional distillation without using the words evaporation and condensation.
Naming fractions beyond those the specification lists, and getting them wrong.
Saying finite means no crude oil is forming, rather than that it forms far more slowly than it is used.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer tests a formula against the general formula rather than recognising it, and says so. It explains fractional distillation as a sequence with evaporation and condensation named, and then makes the link that the column sorts by boiling point and therefore by molecule size, which is why a fraction has a similar number of carbon atoms throughout. It explains the trends rather than listing them, and is careful that boiling overcomes forces between molecules while the covalent bonds inside survive. When asked why a fuel suits a use, it moves from size to property to use in that order, and it recognises that a drawback can be acceptable in one setting and fatal in another.
